title: RELIEF: Reinforcement Learning Empowered Graph Feature Prompt Tuning

problem.claim: Graph feature prompt tuning must determine which nodes to prompt and what feature prompts to attach while seeking downstream performance gains.

gap.claim: Existing approaches either depend on specific pre-training strategies or prompt every node, leaving the necessity of prompting all nodes unresolved.

contributions.claim: RELIEF frames feature-prompt incorporation as a sequential decision-making problem and uses reinforcement learning to optimize it.
The reinforcement-learning agent selects prompted nodes through discrete actions and determines prompt content through continuous actions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On graph- and node-level tasks across various pre-training strategies in few-shot settings, the authors report that RELIEF outperforms fine-tuning and other prompt-based approaches in classification performance and data efficiency.
The authors report that implementation code is available in a public GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: Pre-train, prompt methods have extended generalization and data efficiency to graph representation learning.
Specialized graph prompting depends on particular pre-training strategies, while universal feature prompting raises the unresolved question of whether every node must be prompted.
The paper advocates lightweight prompts on selected nodes, formulates selection and prompt construction as combinatorial optimization, and solves it with reinforcement learning.
Experiments in few-shot graph and node-level tasks reportedly show gains over fine-tuning and other prompt-based approaches in classification performance and data efficiency.

source_observation.claim: The approach uses prompts only on strategically selected nodes rather than adding them to every node.

interpretation.claim: Prompting may benefit from allocating conditioning signal selectively when universal prompting is potentially unnecessary.

application.claim: For graph prompt tuning, consider jointly optimizing prompt locations and prompt content under a task-performance objective.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that selective prompting is preferable for every graph task, model, or pre-training strategy.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, task counts, baseline identities, or quantitative performance gains.
The abstract does not describe the reinforcement-learning algorithm, reward design, training procedure, or computational cost.
The abstract does not provide ablations or details sufficient to assess when prompting fewer nodes is beneficial.
